---
title: "Reliability"
---


The [agreement chapter](agreement.qmd) gives you the coefficients. This one is
about what to do when a coefficient is disappointing, and about the numbers
that have to travel with it before anyone can act on it.

## An interval, always

A coefficient on its own invites over-reading. Qualitative studies work with
few units, so the interval is usually wide, and that is the useful part:

```r
u = qda_units(frag)
ci = qda_bootstrap_ci(u, qda_fleiss)
ci$estimate; ci$lo; ci$hi
```

Units are resampled, not ratings. The unit of analysis is the segment, and
resampling ratings would treat two judgements of one segment as independent
observations.

If fewer than twenty resamples produce a finite value, you get `NULL` instead
of an interval. A wide interval is informative; one computed from almost
nothing is not.

The generator is seeded and is the same one the plugin and the R twin use, so
the interval you publish is reproducible and all three tools agree on it.

## Why the kappa looks like that

Cohen's kappa can collapse while observed agreement is high. Feinstein and
Cicchetti named the two reasons in 1990, and `paradox()` measures both:

```r
d = qda_paradox(qda_units_binary(frag, "Belastung"))
d$prevalence_index; d$bias_index; d$pabak
```

A high **prevalence index** means the agreed-upon cases are lopsided: almost
everything falls in one category, so chance alone explains most of the
agreement. That is the kappa paradox, and it is a property of the measure,
not a fault in your coding.

A high **bias index** is different and more worrying: the two coders differ
systematically, one applying the code more freely than the other. That is
worth a conversation before the next round.

**PABAK** is kappa recomputed with chance fixed at one half, which removes
the prevalence effect. Report it beside kappa, not instead of it. Where the
two diverge, the marginals are the story.

The function returns `NULL` for anything other than two coders and two
categories, because a two-by-two table is what these indices are defined on.

## Which codes were argued about

A pooled coefficient hides where the disagreement sits:

```r
qda_agreement_by_code(frag, min_n = 3)
```

One row per code, most frequent first, each with its own agreement and its
prevalence with a Wilson interval. `min_n` drops codes used fewer times than
that; with two or three uses every coefficient is noise.

This is also the honest treatment of material where a segment legitimately
carries several codes. Each code becomes a separate yes/no question, so a
segment with three codes contributes to three of them instead of being set
aside.

## Prevalence at the edges

```r
qda_wilson(2, 40)
```

Wilson rather than the textbook normal approximation, which Brown, Cai and
DasGupta show to be erratic for small samples and degenerate at nought or
one. Code prevalences live exactly there: a code used in two of forty
segments must not get an interval reaching below zero.

## Did a coder change during the project?

The coding log records who coded what and when, so this question can be asked
at all. Most tools keep no such trail.

```r
qda_code_drift(history, windows = 4)
```

Each row is one coder in one window, with the total variation distance
between their code distribution there and in their first window. Nought means
they are coding as they started; one that the two windows share no code.

Windows hold equal numbers of events rather than equal spans of time, because
a coder who worked in bursts would otherwise get empty ones.

Read it as a description, not a test. A large distance can mean the coder
drifted, or simply that the later material was about something else. Look at
what was coded before concluding anything.
